items.reason: Adapts an online-shopping nudge experiment to three non-generative decision models, testing how defaults and social-influence information affect their choices. items.title: Green Tastes, Beliefs, and Portfolios: Evidence from Synthetic Investors
items.norm_title: green tastes beliefs and portfolios evidence from synthetic investors
items.reason: Uses an LLM as synthetic survey respondents to elicit investors' green preferences, return expectations and portfolio allocations (the authors include Pastor of Booth). The simulated population is investors rather than consumers, and the abstract does not say whether it is compared with a real survey, so uncertain.
items.llm_use: LLMs act as synthetic survey respondents (480 retail and 60 institutional investor identities)
items.human_data: Only compared loosely with real-world green demand and attention measures; no human survey stated
items.classification: Uses an LLM as synthetic investor respondents to elicit green preferences, beliefs and portfolio allocations and reconstruct them across years; a demonstration of simulated surveys that proposes no new estimation method and is not a systematic validity test against humans, similar to Horton's Homo Silicus, placed in 1.1 rather than 1.2/1.3.
items.verification: Title and author order verified against the Crossref SSRN (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7673158) and NBER (w35982) records; Xindi He's position at the Scheller College of Business is documented in her CV.
issues: The Crossref online date of NBER working paper w35982 is 2026-10, earlier than the SSRN date of 2026-11; a decision is needed on which version and month to cite
The SSRN and NBER pages were both inaccessible, and the affiliations were not confirmed on the paper page; Pastor's Booth affiliation is based on prior knowledge.
